Welcome to Module 6. In this module, we are going to move from writing small pieces of Python code toward organizing larger programs in a cleaner and more reusable way.

Up to this point, you have worked with variables, conditions, loops, functions, lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets. Those tools are very useful, but as a program becomes larger, we also need a way to organize the code itself. If everything is placed inside one long script, the program can become difficult to read, difficult to test, and difficult to update.

This module introduces four important ideas. The first is a module. A module is usually one Python file that contains reusable code. The second is a package. A package groups related modules together. The third is a class. A class is a blueprint that combines related data and behavior. The fourth is an object. An object is one actual instance created from a class.

The goal is not to become an advanced software engineer in this module. The goal is much simpler. I want you to understand how Python projects can be organized as they grow.

You will see several executable Python examples throughout the slides. When you reach a code slide, you can click the Run button below the editor. The first time you run Python in the browser, it may take a few seconds for the Python environment to load. After that, the code should run more quickly.

As you move through the module, focus on the big idea behind each example. We want code that is easier to reuse, easier to understand, and easier to maintain.

Before we begin the technical material, let us quickly review how to use this interactive lesson.

Each slide contains one main idea. Some slides explain a concept, and other slides contain executable Python code. You can move through the lesson by using the Next and Previous buttons, the arrow keys, or the slide menu at the top of the page.

When you reach a code example, first read the explanation above the editor. Then look through the code from top to bottom. Try to predict what the code will do before you run it.

When you are ready, click the Run button. The result appears in the terminal area below the code. Compare the terminal output with what you expected.

After that, make a small change. For example, change one number, one name, or one input value. Then run the cell again and see how the output changes. Small experiments are one of the best ways to learn programming.

If you accidentally change the code too much, you can use the Reset button to restore the original example. You can also use the Copy button if you want to paste the example into Jupyter Notebook, Google Colab, or Visual Studio Code.

One important detail is that the spacebar will not move to the next slide while you are editing code. This means you can type normally inside the editor.

The basic workflow for this module is simple. Read the idea. Run the code. Check the output. Change something small. Then apply the same pattern to a new example.

This slide shows the learning path for Module 6.

We will begin with imports. An import allows Python to use code that is stored somewhere else. We will start with modules that are already included with Python, such as math, random, datetime, and statistics.

Next, we will look at how to create our own module. This is an important step because it shows how one Python file can provide reusable functions to another Python file.

After that, we will discuss packages. A package is a folder that groups related modules together. We will also distinguish between a module, a package, and a library. This will prepare you for later modules when we begin using larger tools such as NumPy and Pandas.

Then we move into object-oriented programming. We will introduce classes, objects, attributes, methods, and the word self. We will keep these ideas simple and practical.

You will also see how one class can create multiple objects. For example, one Product class can create a laptop object, a monitor object, and many other product objects. Each object can store its own values while using the same class definition.

Finally, we will compare functions, dictionaries, modules, and classes. The goal is to help you decide which structure is appropriate for a particular task.

The key idea for the entire module is organization. We are learning how to give related code a clear home so that an analytics project can grow without becoming one large and confusing script.

Let us begin with a basic question. Why do we need to organize code at all?

For a very small script, organization may not seem important. If your program is only ten or twenty lines long, putting everything in one file may be perfectly fine.

But analytics projects often grow. You may start with a few calculations, then add data cleaning, summary statistics, visualizations, helper functions, reports, and perhaps a predictive model. Over time, one file can become hundreds or even thousands of lines long.

When everything is stored in one place, several problems can appear. It becomes harder to find the part of the program you need. A change in one area may accidentally affect another area. Repeated code may appear in several places. Team members may have difficulty understanding which section is responsible for which task.

Organized code gives related work a clear home. For example, financial calculations can live in one module. Data-cleaning functions can live in another module. A class that represents a customer can live in another file.

This organization is useful for teams, but it is also useful when you work alone. Imagine returning to a project three months later. A clean structure helps you understand your own work much more quickly.

So when we talk about modules, packages, and classes, we are not adding complexity just for the sake of complexity. We are using structure to make larger programs easier to understand, reuse, test, and maintain.

A module is one of the simplest ways to organize Python code.

In practical terms, a module is usually a Python file with a dot P Y extension. That file can contain functions, variables, constants, or classes that another Python file can use.

Python also comes with many built-in modules. One example is the math module. If we write import math, Python makes the tools inside the math module available to our program.

After importing the module, we can access its contents by using the module name, followed by a dot. For example, math dot square root gives us access to the square root function stored inside the math module.

If we calculate math dot square root of eighty-one, the result is nine.

A useful way to think about a module is as a toolbox. The module is the toolbox, and the functions inside it are the tools. Importing the module is like bringing the toolbox into your workspace. Then you choose the tool you need.

This approach is useful because we do not need to rewrite common functionality. Python already provides modules for mathematics, random values, dates and times, statistics, file handling, and many other tasks.

Later, we will also create our own module. The same idea applies. We place reusable code in a separate Python file and then import that file when we need its functions.

Now we will run our first code example for this module.

This cell imports three tools from Python's standard library. The first line imports the math module. The second line imports the random module. The third line imports only the date class from the datetime module.

Notice that the third import uses a slightly different style. Instead of importing the entire datetime module, we say from datetime import date. This gives us direct access to date without writing datetime dot date every time.

Next, the variable number is assigned the value eighty-one. The program then calculates the square root by calling math dot square root and stores the result in a variable named root.

The next line uses random dot sample. It chooses three values from a range of identification numbers between one thousand and one thousand nine. Because this is random, your result may be different each time you run the cell.

The program then uses date dot today to get today's date from the computer environment.

Finally, the print statements display four results. The first should show a square root of nine point zero. The second displays pi rounded to three decimal places, which should be approximately three point one four two. The third displays three randomly selected identification numbers. The final line displays today's date.

Go ahead and click the Run button now. If Python is loading for the first time, wait a few seconds. Then look at the terminal output below the code.

Pay attention to the random sample. Run the cell a second time. The square root and rounded pi should remain the same, but the sample identification numbers may change.

For a small experiment, change the number from eighty-one to one hundred forty-four. Run the cell again. The square root should now be twelve point zero.

This example demonstrates an important idea. By importing standard-library modules, we can use reliable tools that already exist instead of writing everything ourselves.

Python gives us more than one way to import code.

The first style is to import the entire module. For example, import math. When we use this style, we usually write the module name before the function, such as math dot square root.

The second style is to use an alias. An alias gives a module a shorter name. For example, import statistics as stats. After that, we can write stats dot mean instead of statistics dot mean.

Aliases are especially common in data analytics. Later in the course, you will often see NumPy imported as N P and Pandas imported as P D. These aliases are widely recognized by Python users.

The third style is a selective import. For example, from math import square root. This imports one specific function directly. After that, we can call square root without writing the module name first.

There is no single import style that is always best. The choice depends on readability.

If you need several tools from the same module, importing the whole module is often clear. If a short alias is standard and easy to recognize, an alias can make the code easier to read. If you only need one specific function, a selective import can be convenient.

The important rule is to keep the code understandable. Do not create unusual aliases just to save a few characters. Shorter code is not automatically better code.

This example uses an alias with Python's statistics module.

The first line says import statistics as stats. This means that for the rest of the program, we can refer to the statistics module using the shorter name stats.

Next, we create a list called scores. The list contains five values: eighty-two, ninety, seventy-six, eighty-eight, and ninety-five.

Then we calculate several summary statistics. Stats dot mean calculates the arithmetic average. Stats dot median calculates the middle value after the scores are ordered.

We also use the built-in minimum and maximum functions to find the smallest and largest values. The range is calculated by subtracting the lowest score from the highest score.

Before you run the code, try to predict some of the output. The highest score is ninety-five. The lowest score is seventy-six. Therefore, the range should be nineteen.

Now click the Run button.

You should see the original list of scores. The average should be eighty-six point two. The median should be eighty-eight. The range should be nineteen.

This is a small example, but it represents a common analytics pattern. We start with a collection of values, then use reusable functions to summarize the data.

Now try a small change. Add another score to the list, such as one hundred. Run the cell again and observe how the average, median, and range change.

The main lesson is not the specific numbers. The lesson is that an alias can make repeated use of a module more readable while still making it clear where the functions come from.

So far, we have imported modules that already exist. Now we will look at the idea of creating our own module.

Suppose we are working on an analytics project that repeatedly calculates profit and profit margin. We could write those formulas again and again in the main program, but that creates repetition.

A better approach is to create a separate file called calculations dot P Y. Inside that file, we can define functions such as calculate profit and profit margin.

Then we create another file, perhaps main dot P Y. The main file imports the calculations module and uses those functions when needed.

This creates a clear separation of responsibilities. The calculations file stores reusable formulas. The main file focuses on the current analysis.

This is useful because the main program becomes shorter and easier to read. It is also easier to update the formula later. If we change the calculation in one module, every script that imports that module can use the updated logic.

A beginner-friendly rule is this. When one script starts to contain many useful helper functions, consider moving related functions into their own module.

You do not need to create a separate file for every tiny function. The goal is not to break a project into dozens of unnecessary files. The goal is to group related code in a way that makes the project easier to understand.

This code demonstrates the idea of creating and importing your own module directly inside the browser.

Because this interactive lesson runs in a browser-based Python environment, the example first creates the contents of a module as text. That text contains two functions.

The first function is calculate profit. It receives sales and costs, then returns sales minus costs.

The second function is profit margin. It first calls calculate profit, then divides the profit by sales. This is a good example of one function reusing another function.

Next, the code opens a file named calculations dot P Y in write mode and writes the module text into that file. At this point, a real Python module file exists in the browser's temporary Python environment.

The code then imports importlib and imports the calculations module. Importlib dot reload is used so that if you edit the module text and run the cell again, Python reloads the updated version.

After that, sales is set to fifteen hundred and costs is set to eleven hundred.

The first print statement calls calculations dot calculate profit. The expected profit is four hundred.

The second print statement calls calculations dot profit margin. Four hundred divided by fifteen hundred is approximately zero point two six seven when rounded to three decimal places.

Click Run now and check the terminal output.

You should see Profit followed by four hundred, and Profit margin followed by approximately zero point two six seven.

Now change sales to two thousand and costs to sixteen hundred. Run the code again. The profit is still four hundred, but the profit margin changes because four hundred is now a smaller percentage of total sales.

This is an important idea. A module lets us separate reusable formulas from the main analysis. In a real project, calculations dot P Y and main dot P Y would usually be separate files in the project folder.

A package is the next level of organization above a module.

Remember that a module is usually one Python file. A package is usually a folder that groups related Python modules together.

Imagine that you are building a larger analytics project. You might have one module for finance calculations, one module for health-related calculations, and one module for reporting tools. Instead of leaving all of those files loose in the main project folder, you can group them inside a package folder.

This makes the project structure easier to understand. When someone looks at the folder, they can immediately see which files belong together.

Traditionally, Python packages often contain a special file named dunder init dot P Y. Modern Python can support some package structures without that file, but you will still see dunder init dot P Y in many real projects.

For this introductory module, you do not need to build a complicated package. The main goal is to understand the hierarchy.

A module is generally one file. A package is a folder of related modules. A library is a broader collection of reusable tools that may contain multiple packages and modules.

Later, when we use libraries such as NumPy and Pandas, this terminology will make more sense because you will see how large collections of Python tools are organized.

This slide compares three terms that are sometimes used loosely: module, package, and library.

A module is the smallest of the three concepts in this comparison. It is usually one Python file that contains reusable code. Examples include the built-in math module or a file that we create ourselves, such as calculations dot P Y.

A package is a folder that groups related modules. For example, a package named analytics could contain finance dot P Y, health dot P Y, and reporting dot P Y.

A library is a larger collection of reusable tools. Libraries may contain several packages and many modules. NumPy and Pandas are good examples of widely used libraries in data analytics.

A simple way to remember the relationship is this. Module means file. Package means folder. Library means a larger reusable collection of tools.

The exact technical details can become more complicated in professional software development, but this simple model is enough for our course.

Use a module when one file can hold a related set of functions or constants. Use a package when the project contains several related modules that should be grouped together. Use a library when a larger collection of reusable tools is shared across many tasks or projects.

As we move into NumPy and Pandas later in the course, you will see that importing a library gives us access to many organized tools that other developers have already created and tested.

This code cell contains several related helper functions. Even though they are shown in one interactive cell, you can imagine that these functions live inside a small module called metrics tools dot P Y.

The first function is get profit. It receives sales and costs and returns the difference.

The second function is get profit margin. Notice that it does not repeat the profit formula. Instead, it calls get profit. This is good design because the profit calculation has one clear home.

The third function is format percent. It receives a decimal value, multiplies it by one hundred, and formats the result with one decimal place followed by a percent sign.

Below the function definitions, sales is set to twenty-five hundred and costs is set to eighteen hundred.

The program calculates profit and stores it in the variable profit. It also calculates the profit margin and stores it in the variable margin.

Before running the cell, let us predict the result. Twenty-five hundred minus eighteen hundred equals seven hundred. The profit margin is seven hundred divided by twenty-five hundred, which is zero point twenty-eight, or twenty-eight percent.

Click Run now.

The terminal should show Profit followed by seven hundred. It should also show Profit margin followed by twenty-eight point zero percent.

Now change sales or costs and run the example again. For example, keep sales at twenty-five hundred but change costs to two thousand. The profit becomes five hundred and the margin becomes twenty percent.

The important idea is organization. Related helper functions can be placed together in a module. Then the main analysis can focus on the data and the questions instead of repeating formulas.

Now we move from modules and packages into the basics of object-oriented programming.

The most important new term is class.

A class is a blueprint. It describes what information an object should store and what actions that object should be able to perform.

Think about a product in an analytics system. Every product may have a name, a price, and a category. A product may also need actions such as calculating a discounted price or updating inventory.

Instead of storing the data in one place and the related functions somewhere else, a class can keep the data and behavior together.

For example, we might define a class named Sale. The class describes what every Sale object should contain.

After defining the class, we can create an object from that blueprint. An object is one actual instance. If the class is Sale, one object might represent the sale of a notebook, while another object might represent the sale of a laptop.

The class itself is not the data record. It is the definition or blueprint. The objects created from the class hold their own values.

For this course, we will keep classes simple. We will focus on attributes, which store data, and methods, which perform actions using that data.

This is our first complete class example.

The class is named CustomerRecord. By convention, Python class names are often written using capital letters at the beginning of each word.

Inside the class, we define a special method called dunder init. Its written form uses two underscores before init and two underscores after it. You will often hear Python developers simply say dunder init.

The dunder init method runs when a new object is created. In this example, it receives self, customer ID, and segment.

The word self refers to the current object. When we write self dot customer ID equals customer ID, we are storing the provided customer ID inside the object. The same idea applies to self dot segment.

Next, the line that creates CustomerRecord with C one zero one and Retail creates one object. That object is stored in the variable customer.

The final two print statements access the object's attributes using customer dot customer ID and customer dot segment.

Before you run the code, predict the output. The customer ID should be C one zero one, and the segment should be Retail.

Click Run now.

The terminal should display those two values.

Now try creating a second object. For example, you could create another CustomerRecord with the ID C one zero two and the segment Business. Then print the second object's attributes.

The key idea is that the class defines the structure, while each object stores its own values.

A class becomes especially useful when we create multiple objects from the same blueprint.

Imagine a Product class. The Product class might define two attributes: name and price. It might also define a method that calculates a sale price.

From that one class, we can create many objects.

One object could represent a laptop with a price of nine hundred dollars. Another object could represent a monitor with a price of three hundred dollars. A third object could represent a keyboard, and so on.

All of these objects follow the same structure because they come from the same Product class. However, each object stores its own values.

This is similar to using the same blank form for many records. The form has the same fields, but each completed form contains different information.

Methods also work with the values stored in each object. If the Product class has a sale price method, the laptop object uses the laptop's price, while the monitor object uses the monitor's price.

This separation is important. The class provides the common blueprint. The objects represent individual instances.

In analytics, this pattern can be useful when we want to model repeated entities such as customers, products, patients, locations, transactions, experiments, or model configurations.

This code shows how one class can create two separate objects.

We define a class named Product. The dunder init method receives a name and a price and stores them as self dot name and self dot price.

The class also contains a method named sale price. A method is simply a function that belongs to a class.

The sale price method receives a discount rate. It multiplies the object's price by one minus the discount rate.

Next, we create item one. Item one is a Product object representing a laptop with a regular price of nine hundred dollars.

Then we create item two. Item two represents a monitor with a regular price of three hundred dollars.

Notice that both objects use the same Product class, but they store different values.

The print statements display each product's regular price and its sale price using a ten percent discount.

Before running the code, let us predict the results. Ten percent of nine hundred is ninety, so the laptop sale price should be eight hundred ten dollars. Ten percent of three hundred is thirty, so the monitor sale price should be two hundred seventy dollars.

Click Run now and confirm those results in the terminal.

Next, try creating a third object. For example, create a Product named Keyboard with a price of one hundred. Then print its sale price using the same ten percent discount.

This demonstrates one of the central ideas of object-oriented programming. We define the behavior once in the class and reuse it across many objects.

Now let us focus more closely on methods and the word self.

An attribute is data stored inside an object. For example, self dot price stores a price that belongs to the current object.

A method is a function that belongs to a class. For example, a method named total might multiply price by quantity.

The word self refers to the current object that is using the method.

Suppose we have two Sale objects. One sale contains a notebook with a quantity of four. Another sale contains a pen with a quantity of ten.

When we call the total method on the notebook sale, self refers to the notebook sale object. When we call the same method on the pen sale, self refers to the pen sale object.

This is why one method can work with many different objects. The method definition is shared, but self connects the calculation to the correct object's data.

At first, self may feel unusual. A useful way to read self dot price is this object's price. Read self dot quantity as this object's quantity.

When you see a method such as total with self inside it, think of the method as saying, use the values stored in this particular object.

You will see this idea again in the next code example.

This example creates a Sale class that combines stored data with a calculation.

The dunder init method receives an item, a price, and a quantity. These values are stored as self dot item, self dot price, and self dot quantity.

The class also defines a method named total. The total method returns self dot price multiplied by self dot quantity.

Notice that total does not need the price and quantity to be passed again. Those values are already stored inside the object.

Next, we create one Sale object. The item is Notebook, the price is twelve dollars and fifty cents, and the quantity is four.

The print statements display the item name, the quantity, and the result of calling sale dot total.

Before running the cell, calculate the total yourself. Twelve dollars and fifty cents multiplied by four equals fifty dollars.

Click Run now.

The terminal should show Notebook as the item, four as the quantity, and a total of fifty dollars formatted with two decimal places.

Now change the quantity from four to six and run the cell again. The total should change automatically because the method uses the object's current price and quantity.

You can also change the price and observe the result.

The main idea is that related data and behavior stay together. The Sale object stores the details of the sale, and its total method performs a calculation that belongs naturally to that sale.

This example brings several object-oriented ideas together in a small analytics class.

The class is named SalesReport. Its purpose is to store a collection of sales values and provide several related summary calculations.

The dunder init method receives a list of sales and stores it in self dot sales.

The first method is total sales. It returns the sum of all values in the list.

The second method is average sale. It adds all sales values and divides by the number of values.

The third method is high sales count. This method receives a cutoff value. It starts a counter at zero, loops through each sale, and increases the counter whenever a sale is greater than or equal to the cutoff. Finally, it returns the count.

Next, we create one SalesReport object using the values one hundred twenty, two hundred fifty, one hundred seventy-five, three hundred twenty, and ninety.

Before you run the cell, let us predict the output.

The total of these five values is nine hundred fifty-five. The average is one hundred ninety-one. If the cutoff is two hundred, only two values meet or exceed the cutoff: two hundred fifty and three hundred twenty.

Click Run now.

The terminal should show total sales of nine hundred fifty-five, an average sale of one hundred ninety-one point zero, and two sales at least two hundred.

Now change the cutoff in the final line from two hundred to one hundred fifty. Run the cell again. More values should now meet the threshold.

This example shows when a class can be useful in analytics. The data and several repeated actions belong together. The SalesReport object stores the sales values and provides methods that summarize those values.

At this point, you may be wondering when you should use a function, a dictionary, or a class.

There is no need to use a class for every problem. In fact, the simplest structure that clearly solves the problem is usually the best choice.

Use a function when you mainly need to perform one reusable task. For example, a function called get profit can receive sales and costs and return the profit.

Use a dictionary when you mainly need to store related values. For example, a product dictionary might store a product name, price, and category.

Use a class when the data and the behavior naturally belong together. For example, a Product class can store a name and price and also provide a sale price method.

A class is especially useful when you expect to create many objects of the same type or when several methods need to work with the same stored data.

But classes also add structure, so do not use them simply because they look more advanced.

A good beginner rule is to start simple. If a function is enough, use a function. If you only need to store related values, a dictionary may be enough. Move to a class when one concept clearly has both stored data and repeated actions.

The goal is readable code, not the most complicated code.

This slide brings together the main organization tools from the module.

A function is best for one reusable task. For example, get profit can calculate profit whenever we provide sales and costs.

A module is best when we have a file containing related functions, classes, or constants. For example, metrics dot P Y could store several reusable business metrics.

A package is useful when several related modules belong together. For example, an analytics tools package might contain separate modules for finance, health, and reporting.

A class is useful when related data and behavior belong together. SalesReport is a good example because it stores sales data and provides methods that summarize that data.

An object is one actual instance created from a class. For example, report equals SalesReport with a list of values creates one specific report object.

A useful progression for beginners is this. Start with functions. When a file becomes too long or contains several related helpers, move related code into modules. When you have several related modules, consider a package. Use classes when a concept has its own data and repeated behaviors.

Real projects may combine all of these tools. A package can contain several modules. A module can contain functions and classes. A class can contain multiple methods. The structures work together rather than competing with one another.

The most important question is always the same: which structure makes this project easier to understand and maintain?

Let us finish Module 6 by reviewing the main ideas.

A module is usually one Python file that contains reusable code. Python provides many built-in modules, and we can also create our own modules.

An import statement gives a program access to code from another module. We can import a complete module, use an alias, or selectively import a specific tool.

A package is a folder that groups related modules together. Packages become useful as a project grows and contains several related files.

A class is a blueprint for creating objects. The class describes the attributes an object stores and the methods it can perform.

An object is one actual instance of a class. One class can create many objects, and each object can store its own values.

Attributes are data stored inside an object. Methods are functions that belong to a class. The word self refers to the current object and allows a method to use that object's own attributes.

Remember that you do not need to use classes everywhere. Use the simplest structure that clearly fits the task.

For additional practice, try creating a class named StudentScore. Give it a student name and a list of scores. Then create a method that calculates the average score. After that, create two StudentScore objects with different values and print the average for each object.

If you can explain the difference between a module, a package, a class, and an object, and if you can read the class examples in this module, then you have reached the main goal.

The larger lesson is organization. As analytics projects grow, good structure makes code easier to reuse, easier to test, easier to explain, and easier to maintain.

In the next module, we will continue building our Python skills with more advanced programming techniques.
